narrative:
Your application was denied because the model estimated a 56% chance that you would fail the bar exam on the first attempt—slightly more likely to fail than to pass. That probability drove the rejection; it is not a statement that failure is certain, but it means the model’s risk estimate fell on the unfavorable side of the decision threshold.

The strongest factor was your third-year class standing. You were in the first decile, while accepted students averaged around the fifth-to-sixth decile, and this was the single most influential feature, pushing the prediction toward bar-exam failure. Your first-year standing was also below the accepted-student average, but its influence ranked second and it actually pushed toward passing. Family income ranked third: coming from a lower-middle-income household, relative to the mostly upper-middle- and middle-income accepted group, also pushed slightly toward passing.

To strengthen a future application, focus on what you can change: seek admissions guidance about whether an appeal or updated academic record is possible, consider whether retaking the LSAT is advisable, and provide context for your third-year performance. A stronger recent academic record and test score would be the most direct way to reduce the model’s estimated risk.
